reference.one_line: 84-year-old woman with mild dementia, day 1 after cemented right hemiarthroplasty for a femoral neck fracture; new delirium, uncontrolled pain, haemoglobin 8.6, rehabilitation placement pending.

handoff.summary: Ottoline Hallworth, 84, 52 kg, mild Alzheimer-type dementia, had a right cemented hemiarthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia on 16 Nov after a fall at home. Delirium began at 23:40 on 16 Nov, 95 minutes after diphenhydramine 25 mg, and she is still inattentive and knows person only. Pain is 6 to 7 out of 10, and two overlapping orders have delivered 4,975 mg of acetaminophen since 15:05 yesterday. Haemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL (12.1 on arrival) with a dry dressing, sodium is 131 mmol/L and bowels last opened on 14 Nov. Geriatric medicine's recommendations from 11:40 are not yet ordered; son Desmond is health care proxy, full code.
to_do: Get diphenhydramine discontinued before tonight (still active)
Before the 15:00 acetaminophen, ask the resident to change to 1,000 mg every 8 hours and swap hydrocodone-acetaminophen for oxycodone 2.5 mg as needed
Pain relief 30 minutes before physiotherapy; stand only with frame and two people
Suppository today if no bowel movement
Recheck bladder (180 mL passed at 11:00, 140 mL residual)
Blood count and chemistry on 18 Nov; stop intravenous fluid once drinking; start vitamin D
Bed alarm, low bed, glasses and hearing aids, son at bedside; no restraints or sedatives
if_then: If haemoglobin is below 8 g/dL tomorrow or she becomes symptomatic, then transfuse red cells
If she cannot settle tonight, then use reorientation, low light and family presence and call the resident; do not give diphenhydramine, a benzodiazepine or tramadol
If the dressing shows fresh blood, the thigh becomes tense or the foot turns cold or numb, then call the orthopaedic resident at once
If she has not passed urine again by early evening, then repeat the bladder scan and tell the resident

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mrs Hallworth is an 84-year-old woman with mild Alzheimer-type dementia, osteoporosis and hypertension who lives with her son. She fell in her kitchen at about 16:30 on 15 Nov and arrived by ambulance at 17:40. X-ray showed a displaced right femoral neck fracture and CT head showed no acute injury. A groin nerve block was placed in the emergency department, and lisinopril and alendronate were held. On 16 Nov she had a right cemented bipolar hemiarthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia (incision 08:42, closure 09:50, blood loss 250 mL, no complications); the X-ray afterwards showed a well-positioned implant. Cefazolin was completed and enoxaparin 40 mg nightly was started at 22:00 for a planned 28 days. That evening she asked for a sleeping tablet and received diphenhydramine 25 mg at 22:05. At 23:40 she became acutely confused and agitated, and she remains delirious on day 1. Geriatric medicine attributes this to the antihistamine, uncontrolled pain (scores of 6 to 7 overnight), constipation, anaemia and low sodium, and advises stopping diphenhydramine, limiting acetaminophen to 3 g a day and replacing the hydrocodone combination tablet with oxycodone 2.5 mg; these changes are not yet ordered. Haemoglobin has fallen from 12.1 to 8.6 g/dL without visible bleeding and sodium is 131 mmol/L. Urinalysis was bland and the catheter was removed at 06:15 on 17 Nov. She stood and took 4 steps with a frame and two assistants. Inpatient rehabilitation is anticipated.

qa.q: What weight and kidney function should be used to dose her medicines?
qa.a: 52.0 kg; creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, estimated clearance about 38 mL/min.

qa.q: What opioid has she had since returning from theatre?
qa.a: Three hydrocodone-acetaminophen 5 mg/325 mg tablets: 16 Nov 21:50, 17 Nov 06:20 and 10:05.

qa.q: Has she passed urine since the catheter was removed?
qa.a: Yes: 180 mL at 11:00, with 140 mL left on the scan afterwards. The catheter came out at 06:15.

qa.q: How has her haemoglobin changed since arrival?
qa.a: 12.1, 11.6, 9.4, then 8.6 g/dL on 17 Nov at 05:40: a fall of 3.5 g/dL.

qa.q: What are her sodium and fluid balance doing?
qa.a: Sodium 136, 135, then 131 mmol/L. She is positive every shift (+540, +500, +690 mL) while drinking only 120 to 310 mL a shift.

qa.q: What were her pain scores overnight on 16 to 17 Nov?
When did the confusion actually start?
qa.a: 23:40 on 16 Nov, when she was found with a leg over the bed rail calling for her late husband, 95 minutes after diphenhydramine at 22:05. The progress note's 'about 05:00' is wrong.

qa.q: How long after the spinal and wound closure was the first enoxaparin dose?
qa.a: Given at 22:00 on 16 Nov: 13 hours 40 minutes after the spinal at 08:20 and 12 hours 10 minutes after closure at 09:50.

qa.q: How long was it from the fall to surgery?
qa.a: About 16 hours: fall at roughly 16:30 on 15 Nov (son's estimate), incision 08:42 on 16 Nov.

qa.q: How much acetaminophen has she had in the last 24 hours, and is that acceptable?
qa.a: 4,975 mg between 15:05 on 16 Nov and 10:05 on 17 Nov (four 1,000 mg doses plus three tablets of 325 mg). That exceeds the 3 g a day advised at 52 kg, and 1,000 mg more is due at 15:00.

qa.q: Does she need a transfusion now?
qa.a: No. Haemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL; the plan is to transfuse below 8 or if symptomatic and to repeat the count on 18 Nov.

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: The orthopaedic team was in theatre all afternoon. The 15:00 acetaminophen was given, and at 17:20 the resident entered the pain changes but overlooked the as-needed sleeping tablet. A suppository worked that evening. At 22:10 a float nurse gave diphenhydramine again. At 01:50 on 18 Nov the bed alarm sounded and Mrs Hallworth was found on the floor beside the low bed with her IV pulled out; X-ray and CT head showed no injury. Diphenhydramine was stopped on rounds. Haemoglobin was 7.8 g/dL and she received one unit of red cells. The delirium turned quiet and sleepy and cleared slowly over a week; she ate poorly and could not follow instructions well enough for inpatient rehabilitation. She went to a skilled nursing facility on 24 Nov, walking 6 metres with a frame and one assistant. On 7 Dec she was readmitted for five days with aspiration pneumonia and has not returned home.

portal_messages.subject: Mum awake at 3 a.m. - something to help her sleep?
portal_messages.body: Hello, this is Desmond Hallworth writing for my mother Ottoline. For a couple of weeks she has been waking around 3 in the morning and wandering about the house. Last night I found her in the kitchen with the kettle on. I'm worried she'll fall. Is there a sleeping tablet she could have? The chemist has an over-the-counter night-time one I could pick up tomorrow.
ideal_reply_points: No over-the-counter antihistamine sleep aids or other sedatives: they worsen confusion and falls in dementia
Sleep routine advice and night safety (lights, loose rugs)
Offer a review if it continues

portal_messages.subject: Re: Mum awake at 3 a.m.
portal_messages.body: Dear Mr Hallworth, to confirm our call this morning: please do not give your mother the over-the-counter night-time tablets or any other sleeping tablet. They are antihistamines and in people with memory problems they often cause confusion and falls. Keep her active and in daylight during the day, no tea or coffee after lunch, the same bedtime each night, and a night light in the hall. If the wandering carries on, book a visit.
ideal_reply_points: Clear instruction to avoid antihistamine sleep aids, with the reason

portal_messages.subject: Sleeping tablet still on Mum's list tonight?
portal_messages.body: I've just got home from the ward. As I left, the evening nurse said Mum 'has something written up to help her sleep if she doesn't settle'. The older-people's doctor told me this morning that last night's sleeping tablet probably set off the confusion and that it would be stopped. Can someone please check it has actually been taken off before tonight? I rang the ward but it was engaged. She was calmer this afternoon and I don't want her going backwards.
ideal_reply_points: Act tonight: check the orders and get diphenhydramine discontinued before the night round
Confirm to him that it is stopped
Give the direct ward number; he is welcome to stay overnight

portal_messages.subject: Re: Sleeping tablet still on Mum's list tonight?
portal_messages.body: Dear Mr Hallworth, I am sorry. Your message was not seen until this morning, and you were right to worry. The order had not been removed and your mother was given the tablet again at about ten last night. She became very unsettled and was found on the floor beside her bed just before two. The X-ray and head scan show no injury. The tablet is now stopped for good. I will be on the ward at eleven and would like to talk it through with you in person.
ideal_reply_points: Results of the checks after the fall
Confirm the medicine is stopped; offer to meet the same day

portal_messages.subject: Mum coughing when she drinks and very sleepy
portal_messages.body: I visited the nursing facility this afternoon and Mum isn't right again. She coughs and splutters every time she has her tea, she felt hot to me, and she slept through most of the visit, which is new. Her breathing sounded rattly. The staff said they'd keep an eye on her and that the doctor comes on Tuesday. That feels too long to wait. Should she be seen sooner?
ideal_reply_points: Yes: cough with drinks, fever, drowsiness and noisy breathing need assessment today
Ask the facility to check temperature, oxygen level and breathing rate now and call their on-call doctor or send her to the emergency department
Keep her upright; no thin drinks until assessed

conversation.setting: Bedside on 5 North, 17 Nov at about 11:05, after the physiotherapy session: geriatric medicine consult with the patient's son

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Mr Hallworth? I'm Dr Thornbury-Hale, one of the doctors for older patients. The surgeons asked me to see your mother about the confusion.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: Thank goodness. It's Desmond. She's not right. She is not like this at home.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Tell me what an ordinary day looks like for her.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: She's forgetful, I won't pretend. Gets the date wrong, repeats herself. But she knows me, knows she's in her own house, dresses herself, walks round indoors with no stick...

turns.speaker: Mrs Hallworth
turns.text: Walter? Is that Walter?

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: No, Mum, it's Desmond. Sorry. That's my dad. He died in 2019. She hasn't asked for him in years.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Mrs Hallworth, good morning. Can you tell me where we are just now?

turns.speaker: Mrs Hallworth
turns.text: I'm at home. Who let you in?

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: You're in hospital. You broke your hip. Could you say the days of the week backwards for me, from Sunday?

turns.speaker: Mrs Hallworth
turns.text: Sunday... Saturday... Friday... is the kettle on?

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: That's fine, thank you. Desmond, this is a sudden change on top of her memory trouble. We call it delirium. It isn't the dementia leaping forward, it's the brain reacting to the operation, pain, medicines...

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: Like the pneumonia time? In 2024 she saw children in the room. That was the tramadol.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Very like it, and nobody will give her tramadol. But I need to be straight with you. Last night she asked for something to sleep and was given a tablet called diphenhydramine at about ten. It's an antihistamine.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: A sleeping tablet? Her own doctor told me in August not to. They said those were the worst thing for her.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: They were right. The nurse found her climbing over the bed rail at twenty to midnight, about an hour and a half after it. It's top of my list, and I'm recommending it is stopped.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: So it's the tablet, not the operation?

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: It's rarely one thing. Pain is second. When she stood this morning...

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: She cried out. I was there. Four steps to the chair. And I'd been told she had a comfortable night.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Her scores overnight were six and seven out of ten, so no. She's on regular acetaminophen plus a combination tablet with more acetaminophen hidden in it. At 52 kilos that's too much. I'd give the regular one three times a day and swap the combination for a very small dose of oxycodone, half an hour before physio.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: Won't something stronger muddle her more?

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Fair question. A small dose, 2.5 milligrams, is less of a risk than pain left untreated.

turns.speaker: K. Lindholm-Baptiste RN
turns.text: Sorry to interrupt. She passed 180 at eleven and the scan shows 140 left.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Thank you, that'll do for now. Third, her bowels: nothing since the 14th, so laxatives and a suppository today if need be. Fourth, her blood count, 12.1 when she came in and 8.6 today. That's expected, there's no bleeding, and we give blood if it drops under 8. Her salt is a little low too, 131.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: Should she be having the blood-thinning injection if her blood's low?

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Yes. The low count isn't from the injection, and clots after a hip fracture are a real danger. Forty milligrams is right for her kidneys.

turns.speaker: Mrs Hallworth
turns.text: I want to go home, Desmond.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: I know, Mum. Soon. What can I actually do, Doctor?

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: More than any of us. Glasses on, hearing aids in, curtains open, keep telling her where she is, stay if you can. We won't tie her down or sedate her. Now, tell me back what you've understood.

turns.speaker: Desmond
turns.text: Sudden confusion on top of her memory. Mostly the sleeping tablet and the pain, then bowels, low blood and salt. Stop the tablet, sort the pain properly, check the blood tomorrow. And me being here helps.

turns.speaker: Dr. Thornbury-Hale
turns.text: Exactly. One more thing: her vitamin D is low at 18, so a supplement, and we'll plan a drip treatment for her bones in clinic. Most people improve over days, but with dementia it can take weeks and I can't promise all the way back. I'll see her every day.
